items.title: [FDD Diary #25] The Trap After the Spec
content:
Got a spec. Got a process. Got structure. Got tests.
Thought I was ready.

Six things in the spec.
"Build all of this."
It blew up.

Build six things at once, six things blow up at once.
File sync collided with remote commands.
GPU module tangled with monitoring.
Alerts had nothing to connect to.

A spec is a map.
But you can't walk every road at the same time.

What should I build first?

Everything's important. Everything's needed.
But not at the same time.

Remembered what I wanted in the first place.
Three computers working like one.

GPU sharing? Later.
Auto-recovery? Later.

Right now, one thing.
Send a job from my laptop to the desktop.
Get the result back.

If that works, everything else can be added.
If that doesn't work, nothing else matters.

"Start with the smallest thing."

Heard that a hundred times.
But nobody told me what "smallest" means.

Smallest = fewest features?
No.

Smallest = the moment the experience I wanted is felt even once.

Ten features and no experience? Nothing.
One feature and that experience? That's the beginning.

But what is "the experience"?
What does that even mean?

items.title: [FDD Diary #26] UX Is Not Design
content:
"UX? Isn't that a design term?"
No.

iPhone. Unlock. Tap. Done. Good UX.
iMac. Settings three times. Permission. Update. Bad UX.

UX is not design.
UX is the experience you desperately want.

Open my laptop at a cafe.
Need a file from home.
It's not there.
"Shit."

Eliminating that moment.
That's my UX.

Specs define what to build.
UX defines how you experience it.

"File sync" is a spec.
"Open it at the cafe and it's there" is UX.

Build from the system perspective only:
"Sync success: 1,247 files. 3 conflicts — resolve manually."
Feature runs. But it's infuriating.

Build from the human perspective:
Open the laptop. File's there. Done.
Conflicts? Handled. Message? Don't need it.

"It's there." That's all.

A non-developer can't do code review.
Can't read code.

But experience review? Absolutely.

"Opened it at the cafe. File there?"
There? Pass. Not there? Fail.

Didn't read a single line of code.
But answered "is this what I wanted?"

That's the non-developer's ultimate weapon.
Not code review. Experience review.

XDD. UX-Driven Development.
Code is the AI's job.
I design the experience.

items.title: [FDD Diary #27] AI Gives You Boundaries
content:
"SSH?" "Yes. Not behind NAT."
"Port forwarding?" "Yes. Security risk."
"VPN?" "Yes. Slow."
"QUIC?" "Yes. Blocked on some networks."

Twenty rounds of ping-pong.

Every "no" got a "why."
"No" ten times. "Why" ten times.

AI doesn't give you the answer.
AI tells you one fix for one problem.
Touch a different condition — "that won't work" pops up.

What AI gave me wasn't a solution.
It was a boundary.

Every boundary turned out to be a requirement.

Twenty rounds. Chat gets long.
Most people open a new chat.
Start from scratch.

Wrong.

The conversation itself is the research.
The fight is the data.
Don't throw it away.

Gather the records. Bring them back to AI.
This time AI answers differently.
Because this time there's context.

New chat — AI is a new hire.
Same chat with context — AI is a colleague.
Same AI. Different context.

Conversation history = research data.
"Won't work" = requirement.
Twenty rounds = twenty boundaries = twenty spec conditions.

Don't throw it away.
Don't open a new chat.
Take the fight records and go back.

That's how a non-developer uses AI.
